title: The Bamboo Broken by the Wind
translation: O mathematician, a bamboo standing on level ground, 32 hastas tall, was broken at one point by the force of the wind. Its top touched the ground 16 hastas from its base. Tell me, friend, at how many hastas from the root was it broken?
translation_hi: हे गणितज्ञ, समतल भूमि पर खड़ा 32 हाथ ऊँचा एक बाँस हवा के वेग से एक स्थान पर टूट गया। हे मित्र, उसका सिरा जड़ से 16 हाथ की दूरी पर भूमि को छू गया। बताओ, वह जड़ से कितने हाथ ऊपर टूटा?

words.note: Also 'flute', as in Venugopala. Visarga → र् before द: वेणुर्द्वि.
dvi (2), tri (3): digits are read right to left, so 'two-three' = 32. pani = hand.

words.meaning: from the force of the wind
words.note: pavana (wind) + vega (speed, force). Ablative of cause: 'because of'.
Visarga drops before a consonant: स भग्नः.
Past participle of √bhanj (to break). Hindi भग्न, भंग.
nripa (king) stands for 16 in the word-numeral system; mita = measured.
Past participle of √lag (to stick). Hindi लगना.
Ablative of mula. Same mula as 'square root' in the bee verse!
Visarga drops before a consonant: एष भग्नः.
Locative plural of kara (hand, a unit of length).

grammar: Word numerals (bhuta-sankhya): numbers written as words for things. नृप (king) = 16 by convention. Digits are read right to left, अङ्कानां वामतो गतिः, so द्वि-त्रि = 32. This let poets fit numbers into a meter.
Yan sandhi: हस्तेषु + अङ्ग → हस्तेष्वङ्ग. उ before a different vowel becomes व्.
Ablative of cause: पवनवेगात् 'because of the wind's force'. The ablative means 'from', and also 'because of'.
Consonant sandhi: वेगात् + एक → वेगादेक, मूलात् + एष → मूलादेष. त् → द् before a vowel.
question: At how many hastas from the root did the bamboo break?
solution:
Let the break be x hastas up. The broken part (32 − x) becomes the hypotenuse:

x² + 16² = (32 − x)²  ⟹  256 = 1024 − 64x  ⟹  x = 12 hastas

Bhaskara's rule: x = ½ (h − b²/h) = ½ (32 − 256/32) = ½ (24) = 12

Science link: this is exactly the same rule as the peacock verse (verse 5). Bhaskara spotted that two very different stories share one equation, which is the heart of mathematical modelling. The triangle is 12, 16, 20: the 3, 4, 5 triangle scaled by 4.
